introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 2 (0760), Paper 2 - Cameroon History Since 1800, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2026. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each of the sections. All the questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Regle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each of the sections » (3 sections : A 1800-1922, B 1922-1961, C 1961 to present, 4 questions chacune, numerotation continue 1 a 12). `regles_choix` porte le minimum impose, une regle `parmi 1 sur 4` par section ; la regle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable et est recopiee dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question est imprimee « (25 marks) » et la page de garde dit « All the questions carry equal marks » ; `points` de l'exercice et de la question unique valent 25. Aucun ecart avec le sujet (4 x 25 = 100).

Defauts d'impression du sujet : scan de deux pages (CamScanner) avec filigrane gcerevision.com et bandeau publicitaire, sans incidence sur la lecture, mais avec une legere transparence de texte (verso) en haut de la page 2 et entre quelques questions ; les intitules de section sont imprimes avec un tiret demi-cadratin (« 1800 - 1922 ») recopie avec un tiret simple ; la question 2 est imprimee « succeed to extend » (tournure incorrecte, recopiee telle quelle) ; la question 3 est ambigue (« the results of German annexation by 1884 ») ; la question 6 est maladroite (« indigenous resistance and failure against French rule »). Aucune figure, carte ni document dans le sujet. Page de garde verifiee : ADVANCED LEVEL, History 2, Paper 2 - Cameroon History Since 1800, code 0760, JUNE 2026 (reference GCE26/0760/2/BN).

Aucun corrige officiel : les corriges sont des reponses modeles redigees de memoire, sans acces a une source. Les dates, noms et traites sont ceux de l'historiographie etablie ; les faits dont la precision est moindre sont formules prudemment ou sans chiffre. Aucune citation, statistique ni source n'est inventee. Les corriges sont a relire par un historien du Cameroun avant diffusion.

Question 3 : l'enonce est ambigu (« the results of German annexation by 1884 ») ; le corrige traite les resultats immediats (1884-1885) puis, plus brievement, les suites ulterieures de l'annexion. Les dates sont celles de l'historiographie courante : traite germano-duala du 12 juillet 1884 (protectorat proclame le 14 juillet), arrivee du consul britannique Hewett le 19 juillet 1884 (cinq jours trop tard), premiere lettre des chefs duala a la reine Victoria en 1879, cession d'Ambas Bay a l'Allemagne en 1887. La date exacte du depart des missionnaires baptistes (1886-1887) et les details de l'echange entre Bismarck et Londres sont donnes sans precision. A faire relire par un historien du Cameroun si diffusion.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Analyse the reasons for the lukewarm attitude of the British towards the annexation of Cameroon and the results of German annexation by 1884.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** For several years before 1884 the Duala chiefs (notably King Bell and King Akwa) asked Britain to take over their coast. Britain had missionaries, traders and a long presence there, yet it hesitated. Germany, which had a smaller presence but was quicker, signed a treaty with the Duala chiefs in July 1884 and annexed the territory. This answer explains why Britain was lukewarm and what the German annexation produced.

**1. Reasons for the lukewarm British attitude.**
(a) *Reluctance to bear the cost of empire.* Gladstone's Liberal government disliked costly new colonies. British policy favoured free trade and influence without direct rule: British merchants already dominated the coastal trade, and the government saw no need to pay for an administration.
(b) *Other priorities.* In 1882-1884 Britain was absorbed by the occupation of Egypt, the crisis in the Sudan, South Africa and domestic questions, and had little attention for a small stretch of the Bight of Biafra.
(c) *Priority to the Niger Delta and Lagos.* British interests were concentrated on the Niger and the Oil Rivers, where the palm-oil trade was larger, and on the Lagos colony; the Foreign Office regarded Cameroon as secondary.
(d) *Underestimation of Germany.* British officials did not believe that Bismarck, who until then had been hostile to colonies, was serious. When Germany asked whether Britain held any claims in the area, the British replied slowly and unclearly.
(e) *Slow and divided decision-making.* The Foreign Office, the Colonial Office and the Treasury disagreed and delayed. A treaty-making mission was entrusted to Consul Edward Hewett, who arrived in the Cameroon estuary on 19 July 1884, five days after the Germans had signed their treaty with the Duala chiefs and hoisted their flag.
(f) *Earlier British withdrawal.* Britain had earlier left Fernando Po and had not followed the demands of the Baptist missionary Alfred Saker, who had founded Victoria in 1858, to make the coast a colony. Missionaries and traders (Hatton and Cookson, John Holt and others) pleaded for annexation, but without success.
(g) *German pressure.* German firms (Woermann, Jantzen and Thormaehlen) and the colonial movement pressed Bismarck to act and he sent Gustav Nachtigal, who moved faster than the British.

**2. The German annexation and its results.**
(a) *Treaty and protectorate.* On 12 July 1884 the Duala chiefs Bell and Akwa signed a treaty with the agents of the German firms (Schmidt and Voss), accepting German protection; Gustav Nachtigal confirmed it and proclaimed the protectorate on 14 July. The chiefs thought they were securing a protection that would leave their trade and rights intact.
(b) *Duala disappointment and resistance.* Some Duala chiefs and sections (for example at Hickory Town, led by Lock Priso) refused to accept German authority, and German naval forces defeated them in December 1884. The chiefs lost their position as sovereign rulers and, as the Germans pushed inland, their monopoly of the middleman trade.
(c) *Boundaries and the Berlin Conference.* The annexation was recognised in the course of the Berlin Conference (1884-1885) and the Scramble for Africa. The border with the British Oil Rivers was settled in 1885, and Ambas Bay, held for some time by Britain, was transferred to Germany in 1887.
(d) *Expansion and administration.* Germany set up a colony, Kamerun, with a governor (von Soden from 1885), and began to extend its authority inland through expeditions (Zintgraff, Kund and Tappenbeck and others).
(e) *Economic and social changes.* Plantations (bananas, cocoa, rubber, palm), forced labour, taxes and land seizure appeared; the Baptist missionaries gave way to German missions (the Basel Mission from 1886 and Catholic missionaries from 1890).
(f) *Consequences for Britain.* Britain lost the coast but kept the neighbouring Nigerian territory; British traders and the Baptist mission felt abandoned. Later, in 1914-1916, Britain and France took the colony from Germany and divided it.

**Conclusion.** Britain was lukewarm because it did not want the expense of new colonies, was busy elsewhere, underestimated Germany and acted too slowly. Germany took advantage of this, annexed Cameroon in July 1884 and began a colonial rule that deprived the Duala of their independence and opened the way to the exploitation and penetration of the interior.
